title: One shock, different harvests: testing the limits of an 1816 explanation
question: Why did the 1816 climate shock produce different reported harvest outcomes in the Czech Lands and Korea?
argument: The registered scholarly reconstructions report Czech grain losses and later price pressure alongside good Korean rice harvest classifications in 1816. This contrast challenges a uniform-harvest-failure narrative, but does not isolate why outcomes differed or establish household food access. Tambora remains a contributing climate antecedent; matched local sources are needed to test crop, weather and reporting explanations.
historiography: Compare Brázdil et al. (2016) on Czech weather and subsistence pressure with Kim (2023) on Korean harvest reports. Both are scholarly reconstructions with different evidence and geographical scales; this is a pilot comparison, not a complete literature review.
scope: Czech Lands and Chosŏn Korea, 1816–1817. Separate regional synthesis, Seoul rainfall, Iljik farming dates and administrative crop classifications. No claim about every household.
method: Compare dated observations and their source dependencies. Distinguish contribution from temporal association. Match location, season and reporting units before testing crop or household mechanisms.

counterargument: National crop classifications and paddy tax exemptions do not establish household food access. Seoul rainfall cannot be assigned to Iljik farms, and a scholarly synthesis is not independent authentication of the original diaries.
response: Defend variation in reported outcomes, while suspending the explanation of why local crops recovered or who faced hunger. Different reporting systems could explain part of the contrast.
revision: Comparable local crop and household records that show the apparent contrast arose mainly from classification, incomplete coverage or different periods would change the argument.
chapters: 1. Tambora as a contributing shock. 2. Czech weather, grain and price evidence. 3. Korean crop classification and farming chronology. 4. Reporting differences, household access and the unresolved mechanism.
schedule: Verify scholarly passages first. Locate original diaries and administrative compilation, then seek comparable local grain prices and relief accounts. Log unavailable records and revise the scope before writing a causal conclusion.
researchQuestion: Seek dated local crop, rainfall, grain price and household relief records around Iljik and the Czech case; compare the same months and distinguish assessment policy from food availability.
researchSource: Compare provincial crop calendars, tax records and household food access.
researchPlan: Start from the bibliography and locators in Brázdil et al. and Kim. Request the original Iljik diary and Korean crop assessments, check converted dates and classification criteria, then compare local prices and relief evidence. Access and verification are pending; no new historical finding is claimed.
testArgument: Tambora contributed to a climate shock, but the Czech and Korean reports show that this did not produce a uniform harvest crisis. Regional weather, crop calendars and food access must be investigated separately.
testRival: The apparent regional contrast reflects different crops, reporting criteria and administrative coverage rather than established differences in lived food security.
testOwnPrediction: Comparable local records should show different weather and crop outcomes after controlling for reporting categories.
testRivalPrediction: The contrast should diminish when matching crops, seasons, assessment rules and household records.
testDiscriminator: Compare original local crop and price records using matched dates and categories; cross-check household relief and consumption. These sources are still needed.
testReason: The registered records establish contrasting reports, but cannot distinguish regional mechanisms from differences in recording. I can defend the contrast in reports while suspending causal and household claims.
testRevisedArgument: The registered scholarly reconstructions report Czech grain losses and later price pressure alongside good Korean rice harvest classifications in 1816. This contrast challenges a uniform-harvest-failure narrative, but does not isolate why outcomes differed or establish household food access. Tambora remains a contributing climate antecedent; matched local sources are needed to test crop, weather and reporting explanations.
defenseGap: The unsupported link is the mechanism connecting regional climate to household food access. Matched local weather, crop, price and relief records are needed. The defensible claim is currently a contrast between reports.
defenseRival: Different crops and administrative reporting criteria may account for part of the contrast. Compare like crops, dates, categories and household accounts before favoring a regional mechanism.
defenseRevision: Verify the new record’s creator, date, location, purpose and passage; check whether it is independent of current sources. If credible counterevidence changes the reported contrast, revise the scope and evidence roles rather than dismissing it.
caseLimit: National crop classifications and paddy tax exemptions do not establish household food access. Seoul rainfall cannot be assigned to Iljik farms, and a scholarly synthesis is not independent authentication of the original diaries.
